## 2 Setup repository.

Once you have git installed, or are using some other terminal emulator it is
time to make your first repo.

First, change directory into where ever you would like to keep your project
folder. 

For the purpose of consistency I will use the `~/Documents` folder.

`cd ~/Documents`

Now, create a project directory:

`mkdir ./example_project`

Then change directories into it:

`cd ./example_project`

Then lets initaliaze a new git repository:

`git init`

Then lets list all of files within the current directory:

`ls -a`

You will see that a new directory: `.git/` was created. This is what makes a
directory a git repository. This `.git/` directory is where `git` keeps track of
everything it needs to provide you will all of its functionality.

## 3 Configuration

There is a set of commands to configure git through the command line, we will
start with some basic configuration.

Git comes with configuration on both the global (across repos) and the repo
level. Although, most of the time you will just use the global configuration.


Check to see if your username and email are set:

`git config --get user.name`

`git config --get user.email`

If they are not set, then I reccomend that you change them to your Github
username, and email.

`git config --add --global user.name "github_username_here"`
`git config --add --global user.emil "email@something.com"`

It is also good practice to set your default branch:

`git config --add --global init.defaultBranch master`

It is good to know that when we are configuring git using these commands, git is
just changing some files for us.

Global configs are stored in `~/.gitconfig`

Local configs are stored in `./.git/config`

## Baiscs

Try running `git status` in your new project repository.

This command shows us the current staus of repsitory, it will show you which
files are untracked, staged, and commited.

`untracked` - Git will not track this file.
`staged` - Marked for inculsion in the next commit.
`commited` - Saved to the repositories history.

Lets make our first commit.

Make sure that you are in the root of you project directory:

`pwd`

Now lets make create a new file:

If you are familiar with a terminal based text editor like vim or nano, I
encourage you to use it here. If not, open this file with your favorite text
editor.

Create a new file: `hello.md`

Then write "hello world!" into the file and save it, and head back to our
teminal instnace.

run: `git status`

You will see that the new file "hello.md" that we just created is untracked.

We would like to keep track of "hello.md" so lets run:

`git add hello.md`

Now, check the status again:

`git status`

You will see that "hello.md" is now a staged file.

Now lets save a snapshot of this file, within our project directory. It is
neccesary that we include a message when commiting.


I used the word snapshot because git does not store entire files, nor does it
store the difference between changed files. It is more acurate to view a commit
as a picture, or a screenshot of your project directory at the time of your
commit. 

`git commit -m "Add hello.md"`

The `git commit` command will save a snapshot of the staged files, the argument
`-m` means that the preceding text within the quotation marks will be the commit
message. Our commit message should be short and informative.

A commit will save a snapshot of all of the staged changes, that means multiple
edits across multiple files, as long as the changes are staged with `git add`.
All of these changes are labled as a single commit.

We can view our commit history using the command:

`git log`
